extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of poetry, and general readers learning about poetic forms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and defining characteristics for composing free-verse (nonmetrical, nonrhyming) poetry that follows the natural rhythms of speech rather than a fixed metrical plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonmetrical
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines are nonmetrical; the poet does not adhere to a metrical plan in their composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free-verse lines do not follow a fixed meter. While regular patterns of sound or rhythm can appear, they are not the result of a prescribed metrical scheme. Historical practitioners who explored nonmetrical possibilities include Matthew Arnold and Walt Whitman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonrhyming lines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free verse is characterized by absence of regular end-rhyme schemes; rhyme is not a defining organizing principle of the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closely follow natural rhythms of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines should closely follow the natural rhythms of spoken language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize phrasing and cadence that mirror conversational or speech rhythms rather than artificially imposed metric feet; this quality distinguishes free verse from metrical verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for emergent patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular pattern of sound or rhythm may emerge, but it is not imposed by the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional or accidental patterns of sound, rhythm, or repetition are acceptable and can contribute to the poem's effect, but they differ from intentional adherence to a metrical plan. Examples of 20th-century poets who shaped modern free verse include William Carlos Williams, T.S. Eliot, Ezra Pound, and H.D.
